Aim

This is an update of the Lupus nephritis chapter of the KDIGO
Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular
Diseases published in 2021. [362] Based on the recently published data
in the field, it was decided that a guideline update was required.
The objective of this project was to update the evidence-based
clinical practice guideline for the management of LN. The guideline development methods are described below.


Overview of the process
This guideline adhered to international best practices for guideline
development (Appendix B: Supplementary Tables S2 and S3). [363] This
guideline has been developed and reported in accordance with the
AGREE II reporting checklist. [364]

The processes undertaken for the development of the KDIGO
2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Lupus
Nephritis included:

� Appointing Work Group members and the ERT

� Defining scope of the guideline update

� Implementing literature search strategies to update the evidence
base for the guideline

� Selecting studies according to predefined inclusion criteria

� Conducting data extraction and critical appraisal of the updated
literature


� Updating the evidence synthesis and meta-analysis to include
newly identified studies

� Updating the certainty of the evidence for each outcome

� Finalizing guideline recommendations and supporting rationale

� Grading the strength of the recommendations, based on the certainty of the evidence and other considerations

� Convening a public review of the guideline draft in March 2023

� Amending the guideline based on the external review feedback and
updating the literature search

� Finalizing and publishing the guideline
Commissioning of Work Group and ERT. The KDIGO CoChairs appointed the Work Group Co-Chairs, who then assembled the Work Group, to include content experts in adult
nephrology, epidemiology, and public health. The Work Group was
responsible for writing the recommendations and practice points
and underlying rationale, as well as grading the strength of each
recommendation.

For the 2024 update, the Brown University School of Public
Health Center for Evidence Synthesis in Health was contracted to
update the systematic evidence review and provide expertise in
guideline development methodology. The Brown ERT consisted of a

–
senior physician methodologist who led the ERT for the 2012
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerulonephritis, an adult

–
nephrologist, and a librarian methodologist, all with expertise in
evidence synthesis and guideline development, including for KDIGO
guidelines. Cochrane Kidney and Transplant was contracted to
conduct systematic evidence review and provide expertise in guideline development methodology for the 2021 Guideline.



Defining scope and topics and formulating key clinical
questions. Due to resourcing and the probability of practicechanging studies, clinical questions on effectiveness and safety of
interventions included in the guideline update were limited to RCTs.
Guideline topics and clinical questions focusing on nonrandomized
studies were not included in the guideline update (Supplementary
Table S1). The guideline Work Group, with assistance from the
ERT, determined the overall scope of the guideline. A preliminary list
of topics and key clinical questions was informed by the previous
KDIGO guideline. [362] The majority of clinical questions for this
guideline were based upon RCTs to avoid bias by design. Clinical
questions adhered to the population, intervention, comparator,
outcomes, and study design (PICOD) format (a list of critical and
important outcomes was compiled after voting by the Work Group

[Table 1]). Clinical questions were mapped to existing Cochrane
Kidney and Transplant systematic reviews. These systematic reviews
were updated accordingly. For clinical questions that did not map to
any Cochrane Kidney and Transplant systematic reviews, de novo
systematic reviews were undertaken. The previous guideline was
reviewed to ensure all identified studies were included in the evidence review. [362] Details of the PICOD questions and associated
Cochrane Kidney and Transplant systematic reviews are provided in
Table 2 [121] .

All evidence reviews were conducted in accordance with the
Cochrane Handbook, [365] and guideline development adhered to the
standards of GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
Development, and Evaluation). [366]


Literature searches and article selection. For the KDIGO 2024

Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Lupus Nephritis,
updated literature searches were conducted in MEDLINE (via
PubMed), Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled
Trials. The searches were restricted to records entered into the da
tabases since January 1, 2020. This was done to provide a 6-month
overlap with the prior searches. The searches were conducted on
July 7, 2022 and updated on April 25, 2023. These search updates
included terms for both LN and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) vasculitis (which underwent updating concurrently
with the chapter on lupus nephritis).

The titles and abstracts resulting from the searches were screened
by 2 members of the ERT who independently assessed retrieved
abstracts, and if necessary, the full text, to determine which studies
satisfied the inclusion criteria. Disagreement about inclusion was
resolved by discussion with a third member of the ERT.
For the KDIGO 2021 guideline, a total of 25,925 citations were
screened. Of these, 479 RCTs and 102 observational studies were
included in the evidence review for all diseases. For the 2024 update,
a total of 1556 citations were screened (for both LN and ANCA
vasculitis) (Figure 14). From these, we found 21 new eligible articles
on LN that addressed 16 new RCTs, in 17 publications, and 4 new
analyses of previously included RCTs.

Data extraction. For the KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guide
line for the Management of Lupus Nephritis, data extraction was
performed by 1 member of the Brown ERT and confirmed by the 2
other members of the ERT. The Brown ERT extracted data into the

forms designed by the Cochrane ERT. The Cochrane ERT designed
data extraction forms to capture data on study design, study
participant characteristics, intervention and comparator characteristics, and critical and important outcomes. Any differences in
extraction between members of the ERT were resolved through
discussion. A third reviewer was included if consensus could not be

achieved.

Critical appraisal of studies. The majority of reviews undertaken were intervention reviews that included RCTs. For these re
views, the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool was used to assess individual
study limitations based on the following items [367] :



� Was there adequate sequence generation (selection bias)?

� Was allocation adequately concealed (selection bias)?

� Was knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately prevented during the study (detection bias)?

� Participants and personnel (performance bias)

� Outcome assessors (detection bias)

� Were incomplete outcome data adequately addressed (attrition
bias)?

� Are reports of the study free of suggestion of selective outcome
reporting (reporting bias)?

� Was the study apparently free of other problems that could put it
at risk of bias?

All critical appraisal was conducted independently by 2 members
of the ERT, with disagreements regarding the risk of bias adjudications resolved by consultation with a third review author.
Evidence synthesis and meta-analysis. Measures of treatment
effect. Dichotomous outcome (all-cause mortality, kidney
failure, $50% loss of GFR, infection, malignancy, complete remission/relapse) results were expressed as RR with 95% CI. When
continuous scales of measurement were used to assess the effects of

treatment, such as annual GFR loss, the mean difference (MD) with
95% CI was used.

Data synthesis. Data were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel
random-effects model for dichotomous outcomes and the inverse

variance random-effects model for continuous outcomes. The random
effects model was chosen because it provides a conservative estimate of
effect in the presence of known and unknown heterogeneity. [365]

Assessment of heterogeneity. Heterogeneity was assessed by visual inspection of forest plots of standardized mean effect sizes, and
of risk ratios, and by c [2] tests. A P value of <0.1 was used to denote
statistical heterogeneity, and an I [2] was calculated to measure the
proportion of total variation in the estimates of treatment effect that
was due to heterogeneity beyond chance. [365] We used conventions of
interpretation as defined by Higgins et al. [368]

Assessment of publication bias. We made every attempt to
minimize publication bias by including unpublished studies (for
example, by searching online trial registries). To assess publication
bias, we used funnel plots of the log odds ratio (effect vs. standard
error of the effect size) when a sufficient number of studies were
available (i.e., >10 studies). [365] Other reasons for the asymmetry of
funnel plots were considered.
Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity. Subgroup
analysis was undertaken to explore whether there were clinical differences among the studies that may have systematically influenced
the differences that were observed in the critical and important
outcomes. However, subgroup analyses are hypothesis-forming
rather than hypothesis-testing and should be interpreted with
caution. The following subgroups were considered: baseline kidney
function (GFR, proteinuria, presence of albuminuria, presence of
macroscopic hematuria), histopathologic class of disease, primary
versus secondary forms of disease, sex, and adult versus pediatric.
The test of subgroup differences used the I [2] statistic and a P value of
0.10 (noting that this is a weak test). [365]



Sensitivity analysis. The following sensitivity analyses were
considered:


� Repeating the analysis excluding unpublished studies

� Repeating the analysis, taking account of the risk of bias, as
specified

� Repeating the analysis excluding any very long or large studies, to
establish how much they dominate the results

� Repeating the analysis excluding studies using the following filters:
language of publication, source of funding (industry vs. other),
and country in which the study was conducted.
However, the available data were insufficient to determine the
influence of these factors on the effect size of critical and important

outcomes.

intervention, and outcomes measured in trials and their applicability
to the clinical question of interest; imprecision in the evidence review

Practice Guideline for the Management of Lupus Nephritis, the
existing recommendations were reviewed and revised, as necessary,
and new recommendations were drafted by the Work Group and CoChairs. Recommendations were revised in a multistep process by
email and teleconferences. The Brown ERT participated in these
discussions to ensure consistency with the evidence base and to
provide additional feedback.



The final draft was sent for external public review, and reviewers
provided open-ended responses. Based on the external stakeholder
feedback, the draft was further revised by the Work Group. All Work

recommendation is graded as Level 1, “we recommend” or Level 2,
“we suggest” (Table 5). The strength of a recommendation was
determined by the balance of benefits and harms across all critical
and important outcomes, the grading of the overall certainty of the
evidence, patient values and preferences, resource use and costs, and
considerations for implementation (Table 6).
Balance of benefits and harms. The Work Group and ERT
determined the anticipated net health benefit on the basis of expected benefits and harms across all critical and important outcomes
from the underlying evidence review.
The overall certainty of the evidence. The overall certainty of the
evidence was based on the certainty of the evidence for all critical
and important outcomes, taking into account the relative importance of each outcome to the population of interest. The overall
certainty of the evidence was graded (A, B, C, or D—Table 3).

Practice points
In addition to graded recommendations, KDIGO guidelines now
include “practice points” to help clinicians better evaluate and
implement the guidance from the expert Work Group. Practice points
are consensus statements about a specific aspect of care, and they
supplement recommendations for which a larger quantity of evidence
was identified. They are issued when a clinical question was not
supported by a systematic review, often to help readers implement the
guidance from graded recommendation. Practice points represent the
expert judgment of the guideline Work Group, but they also may be
based on limited evidence. For example, practice points were provided
on monitoring, frequency of testing, dosing adjustments for the
severity of CKD, and use of therapies in specific subgroup populations.



Practice points were sometimes formatted as a table, a figure, or an
algorithm to make them easier to use in clinical practice.


Format for guideline recommendations
Each guideline recommendation provides an assessment of the
strength of the recommendation (Level 1; or Level 2) and the certainty of the evidence (A, B, C, D). The recommendation statements
are followed by Key information (Balance of benefits and harms,
Certainty of the evidence, Values and preferences, Resource use and
costs, Considerations for implementation), and Rationale. Each
recommendation is linked to relevant SoF tables. An underlying
rationale may support a practice point.


Limitations of the guideline development process
The evidence review prioritized RCTs as the primary source of
evidence. For a select number of clinical questions in this
guideline, the ERT undertook a comprehensive evidence review
beyond RCTs. However, these reviews were not exhaustive, as
specialty or regional databases were not searched, and manual
searching of journals was not performed for these reviews. In
the development of these guidelines, no scoping exercise with
patients, limited searches of the qualitative literature, nor
formal qualitative evidence synthesis examining patient experiences and priorities were undertaken. As noted, although
resource implications were considered in the formulation of
recommendations, formal economic evaluations were not undertaken for all topics.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 1
structure.summary: Segment 1 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
# Kidney Health FAQs - Direct Answers

This document contains standard, frequently asked questions about kidney health and their detailed answers. These are designed to provide direct, comprehensive responses to common patient inquiries.

---

## What are the early signs of kidney disease?
In the early stages, kidney disease is often silent. The first signs may not appear until the kidneys are significantly damaged. When symptoms do occur, they can include:
*   Changes in urination frequency (especially at night).
*   Foamy or bubbly urine.
*   Swelling (edema) in the feet, ankles, hands, or face.
*   Unexplained fatigue, weakness, or trouble concentrating.
*   Persistent itching (pruritus).
*   High blood pressure that is difficult to control.
*   Muscle cramps.
*   Loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 2
structure.summary: Segment 2 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## Can kidney disease be cured?
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) usually cannot be cured. However, the progression of the disease can often be slowed or halted entirely with proper medical management and lifestyle changes. The goal is to preserve remaining kidney function for as long as possible. Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), on the other hand, can often be reversed if the underlying cause is treated promptly.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 3
structure.summary: Segment 3 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What should I eat to keep my kidneys healthy?
A kidney-friendly diet varies depending on your stage of disease, but general recommendations include:
*   **Controlling protein:** Eating too much protein can strain the kidneys, but too little can lead to malnutrition. Consult a dietitian.
*   **Limiting sodium (salt):** Helps manage blood pressure and fluid retention. Aim for less than 2,000 mg per day. Avoid processed foods, canned soups, and salty snacks.
*   **Managing potassium and phosphorus:** In later stages of CKD, you may need to restrict foods high in these minerals (like bananas, tomatoes, potatoes, dairy, and nuts) to prevent dangerous build-ups in the blood.
*   **Staying hydrated:** Drink enough water to keep your urine clear, but avoid overhydration if you have been told to restrict fluids.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 4
structure.summary: Segment 4 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## How does high blood pressure affect the kidneys?
High blood pressure (hypertension) is a leading cause of kidney failure. It damages the tiny blood vessels (glomeruli) in the kidneys that filter waste from your blood. When these vessels are damaged, the kidneys cannot function properly. Conversely, damaged kidneys can release hormones that further increase blood pressure, creating a vicious cycle. Keeping blood pressure under control (usually below 130/80 mmHg) is crucial for kidney health.

## Why do I need to manage my blood sugar if I have kidney disease?
Diabetes is the number one cause of kidney failure (Diabetic Nephropathy). High levels of sugar in the blood damage the blood vessels in the kidneys over time, causing them to leak protein into the urine and eventually lose their ability to filter waste. Strict blood sugar control is essential to prevent or slow this damage.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 5
structure.summary: Segment 5 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What does my eGFR (estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate) number actually mean?
Think of your eGFR as a percentage of your overall kidney function. It is a mathematical estimate that tells your doctor how efficiently your kidneys are cleaning waste from your blood. A normal eGFR is typically 90 or higher, meaning your kidneys are working at roughly 90% to 100% capacity.

The number is calculated using a formula that takes into account your age, gender, and the level of creatinine in your blood. As kidney disease progresses, the kidneys lose their filtering ability, and this eGFR number slowly goes down.

Monitoring your eGFR over time is one of the most reliable ways to track your kidney health. A sudden drop might indicate an acute, potentially reversible issue, while a slow, steady decline helps you and your care team plan for the future, adjusting your diet and medications accordingly.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 6
structure.summary: Segment 6 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## My creatinine levels are high. How can I lower them naturally?
Creatinine is a normal waste product created by the daily wear and tear on your muscles. Healthy kidneys continuously filter it out of your blood and dispose of it in your urine. When your kidneys are damaged, they struggle to clear this waste, causing the creatinine levels in your blood to rise.

While many patients want to lower their creatinine "naturally," it is important to understand that creatinine itself isn't the primary enemy—it's just a marker, like a thermometer showing you have a fever. Lowering the number artificially (such as by drastically reducing muscle mass or avoiding exercise) doesn't cure the underlying kidney damage.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 7
structure.summary: Segment 7 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
The best way to manage your creatinine is to protect your remaining kidney function. You can do this by strictly controlling the root causes of kidney damage, such as high blood pressure and diabetes. Eating a balanced, kidney-friendly diet, staying properly hydrated as directed by your doctor, and avoiding over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen will help keep your kidneys stable and prevent creatinine from spiking further.

## Are painkillers safe for my kidneys?
Over-the-counter painkillers known as NSAIDs (Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs) can be harmful to your kidneys if taken regularly or in high doses. This includes ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac. They reduce blood flow to the kidneys and can cause acute kidney injury or worsen chronic kidney disease. Always consult your doctor before taking any pain medication; acetaminophen is often a safer alternative for kidney patients.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 8
structure.summary: Segment 8 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What causes kidney stones and how can I prevent them?
Kidney stones form when certain minerals and salts in your urine, such as calcium, oxalate, and uric acid, become highly concentrated and clump together. Prevention strategies include:
*   **Drinking plenty of water:** Essential to dilute the substances in urine that form stones. Aim for 2.5 to 3 liters daily unless advised otherwise.
*   **Reducing sodium intake:** High salt diets increase the amount of calcium in your urine.
*   **Getting enough dietary calcium:** Interestingly, restricting dietary calcium can *increase* stone risk. It's better to get calcium from food rather than supplements.
*   **Limiting animal protein:** High intake can increase uric acid and calcium levels in the urine.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 9
structure.summary: Segment 9 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What is the difference between CKD and AKI?
*   **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** A gradual loss of kidney function over a period of months or years. It is usually progressive and irreversible, often caused by long-term conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
*   **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** A sudden episode of kidney failure or kidney damage that occurs within a few hours or a few days. It is often caused by a sudden drop in blood flow to the kidneys, direct damage to the kidneys, or a blockage of the urinary tract. AKI is often reversible with prompt treatment.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 10
structure.summary: Segment 10 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What foods do I absolutely need to avoid with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)?
There is no single "renal diet" for everyone, as your needs will change depending on your stage of CKD and your latest lab results. However, universally, reducing sodium (salt) and highly processed foods is the most important step. Excess salt raises blood pressure and forces your kidneys to work harder, so it is best to avoid packaged snacks, canned soups, fast food, and salty condiments.

In later stages of CKD, your doctor may also ask you to limit foods high in phosphorus and potassium. Processed meats, dark colas, and certain packaged foods often contain phosphorus additives that your body absorbs very quickly, which can weaken your bones over time.

A good rule of thumb is to focus on fresh, whole foods cooked at home. This gives you complete control over the ingredients. Remember, "avoid" doesn't always mean "never"—it usually means "strictly limit" based on your doctor's specific advice.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 11
structure.summary: Segment 11 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## How much water should I drink today? Do I need to restrict my fluids?
A common myth is that drinking massive amounts of water will "flush" the kidneys. For early-stage CKD, drinking water when you are thirsty is generally enough. Aiming for a normal daily intake (about 1.5 to 2 liters) is usually fine unless your doctor has specifically advised otherwise.

However, if you are in the later stages of CKD or on dialysis, your kidneys may not remove extra fluid efficiently. Fluid buildup can lead to swelling in your legs (edema), high blood pressure, and a dangerous buildup of fluid in your lungs. In these cases, your doctor will prescribe a strict daily fluid limit.

If you are placed on a fluid restriction, remember that "fluids" include anything that melts at room temperature, such as ice, soup, gelatin, and ice cream. Tracking everything you consume that contains water will become an essential part of keeping your heart and lungs safe.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 12
structure.summary: Segment 12 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## Are high-potassium foods like bananas and potatoes bad for me?
Not necessarily. In the early stages of kidney disease, your kidneys can usually handle potassium well, and eating potassium-rich fruits and vegetables is actually highly recommended to help control blood pressure and protect your heart.

As CKD progresses, however, your kidneys might struggle to filter out excess potassium. High potassium levels in the blood (hyperkalemia) can be very dangerous and cause serious heart rhythm problems. If your lab results show high potassium, your doctor will ask you to limit foods like bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, and certain dals or lentils.

If you love potatoes or other high-potassium root vegetables, you can reduce their potassium content by "leaching" them—soaking diced pieces in warm water before boiling. Always wait for your doctor or dietitian to review your blood tests before cutting these nutritious foods out of your diet.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 13
structure.summary: Segment 13 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## How much protein am I allowed to eat, and should it be plant-based or meat?
The amount of protein you need depends heavily on your specific stage of kidney disease. If you are not on dialysis, your doctor will likely recommend a low-protein diet. Eating less protein reduces the workload on your kidneys and decreases the buildup of waste products (like urea) in your blood.

Conversely, if you are on dialysis (either hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis), you actually lose protein during your treatments. In this case, your dietary needs completely flip, and you will need to eat more high-quality protein to maintain your muscle mass, stay strong, and fight off infections.

Regarding the type of protein, plant-based proteins (like lentils, tofu, beans, and nuts) are highly recommended for CKD patients. They produce fewer waste products for the kidneys to clear and are easier on your body than heavy animal proteins like red meat.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 14
structure.summary: Segment 14 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## Can I still drink coffee or alcohol with kidney disease?
For most people with CKD, drinking coffee in moderation (1-2 cups a day) is perfectly acceptable. Black coffee is naturally low in potassium and phosphorus. However, you need to be cautious with what you add to it—heavy milk, syrups, or artificial creamers can add unwanted phosphorus, potassium, and sugar to your diet.

When it comes to alcohol, moderation is also the key. A small, occasional drink might be fine if your kidney disease is stable and your doctor approves. But excessive alcohol can raise your blood pressure, interact dangerously with your medications, and contribute to dehydration.

It's also important to remember that beverages like coffee and alcohol count toward your daily fluid limit if you are on a fluid restriction. Additionally, if you are managing diabetes alongside CKD, your doctor may advise you to avoid alcohol entirely.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 15
structure.summary: Segment 15 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What does it mean if my doctor says I have protein in my urine (proteinuria)?
Inside your kidneys are millions of microscopic filters called glomeruli. In a healthy kidney, these filters act like a fine sieve, keeping important things like protein inside your bloodstream while letting waste and extra water pass through into your urine.

When these filters become damaged—often due to high blood pressure, poorly controlled blood sugar, or inflammation—they become "leaky." This allows proteins, primarily one called albumin, to slip through the filters and end up in the toilet. If you have significant protein in your urine, you might even notice that it looks unusually foamy or bubbly.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 16
structure.summary: Segment 16 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Finding protein in your urine is a crucial warning sign and often one of the earliest indicators of kidney disease, sometimes appearing long before your eGFR drops. Your doctor may prescribe specific blood pressure medications, which are highly effective at reducing the pressure inside the kidneys and minimizing this protein leak, thereby protecting your kidneys from further harm.

## What are the different stages of kidney disease, and which stage am I in?
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is divided into five stages based on your eGFR number. Stage 1 indicates mild kidney damage with normal function (an eGFR of 90 or higher), while Stage 5 signifies kidney failure (an eGFR of less than 15), where the kidneys can no longer support the body and treatments like dialysis or a transplant become necessary.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 17
structure.summary: Segment 17 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Stages 2, 3, and 4 represent a progressive decline in kidney function. Stage 3 is often the critical point where patients might start to feel mild symptoms like fatigue or changes in urination. This is usually when your healthcare team will closely monitor your diet, introduce specific medications, and check your lab work more frequently to slow the disease's progression.

To know exactly which stage you are in, you will need to check your most recent lab report for your eGFR number or ask your doctor. Because I am an AI chatbot and do not have access to your personal medical records, I cannot tell you your specific stage. Discussing your recent blood tests with your nephrologist is the best way to understand where you stand and what your personalized care plan should look like.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 18
structure.summary: Segment 18 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## Why am I always feeling so tired, weak, and cold?
Your kidneys do much more than just filter waste; they also act as a factory for a special hormone called erythropoietin (EPO). This hormone sends a signal to your bone marrow to produce red blood cells, which carry oxygen to every part of your body.

As kidney disease progresses, the damaged kidneys stop making enough EPO. This leads to a drop in your red blood cell count, a condition known as anemia. With fewer red blood cells, your brain and muscles are starved of oxygen, which explains the profound exhaustion, weakness, and the feeling of being cold even when the room is warm.

Fortunately, this type of anemia is highly treatable. Depending on your lab results, your doctor may prescribe iron supplements, vitamin B12, or special injections (called Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents, or ESAs) that mimic the EPO your kidneys are no longer making, helping you regain your energy.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 19
structure.summary: Segment 19 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What causes the swelling (edema) in my legs and ankles, and how can I reduce it?
Swelling, or edema, happens when your kidneys are no longer able to effectively balance the fluid and sodium (salt) in your body. When the kidneys slow down, excess fluid is retained in your tissues. Because of gravity, this extra water tends to pool in your lower extremities, like your feet, ankles, and lower legs.

Another reason for swelling is the loss of protein in your urine. Protein acts like a sponge in your bloodstream, keeping fluid inside your blood vessels. When protein leaks out through damaged kidneys, the fluid seeps out of the blood vessels and into the surrounding tissues.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 20
structure.summary: Segment 20 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
To reduce edema, the most crucial step is limiting your sodium intake—this means keeping a close eye on hidden salts in restaurant foods, packaged snacks, and traditional high-salt items like pickles and papads. Your doctor may also adjust your fluid intake, advise you to keep your legs elevated when sitting, or prescribe medications called diuretics (water pills) to help your body flush out the excess fluid.

## What are the warning signs that my kidney disease is getting worse?
Kidney disease is often called a "silent" illness because you can lose a significant amount of kidney function before feeling any physical symptoms. However, as toxins and waste products build up in your blood (uremia), you might start to experience a metallic taste in your mouth, a sudden loss of appetite, or persistent nausea and vomiting, especially in the mornings.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 21
structure.summary: Segment 21 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Other major red flags include changes in your urination habits—such as waking up multiple times at night to pee or noticing foamy, bubbly urine. You might also experience worsening swelling in your legs or face, shortness of breath from fluid building up in your lungs, or severe, unexplainable skin itching.

Never wait for these severe symptoms to appear before seeking care. The absolute best way to know if your kidney disease is progressing is through regular, scheduled blood and urine tests. If you ever experience sudden chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or extreme confusion, you should seek emergency medical attention immediately.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 22
structure.summary: Segment 22 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What kind of physical exercise is safe for someone with my stage of CKD?
For the vast majority of patients with Chronic Kidney Disease, regular exercise is not just safe—it is highly encouraged. Staying active helps lower blood pressure, improves blood sugar control, boosts your mood, and maintains the muscle strength you need to stay independent.

The best approach is to start slow and focus on cardiovascular exercises that don't put excessive strain on your body. Brisk walking, cycling, swimming, and light yoga are all excellent choices. Aiming for about 30 minutes a day, most days of the week, is a great goal, but even a 10-minute daily walk is much better than no activity at all.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 23
structure.summary: Segment 23 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
You should always listen to your body and avoid exercising to the point of exhaustion or severe breathlessness. Stay hydrated within your prescribed fluid limits, and avoid heavy weightlifting or intense contact sports unless explicitly approved by your doctor, especially if you have an AV fistula for dialysis or a kidney transplant.

## Does high blood pressure cause kidney disease, or does kidney disease cause high blood pressure?
It is actually a two-way street—they closely drive each other. High blood pressure is one of the leading causes of kidney disease. Over time, the excessive pressure of blood pounding against the delicate, microscopic filters in your kidneys damages them, causing them to scar and fail.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 24
structure.summary: Segment 24 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Conversely, kidney disease also causes high blood pressure. Your kidneys are responsible for regulating your blood pressure by managing fluid levels and releasing certain hormones. When the kidneys are damaged, they often mistakenly signal the body to retain more salt and water, which drives your blood pressure even higher, creating a dangerous cycle.

Breaking this vicious cycle is one of the most critical parts of your treatment plan. Taking your blood pressure medications exactly as prescribed—often drugs known as ACE inhibitors or ARBs, which are especially protective of the kidneys—is the most effective way to slow down the progression of CKD.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 25
structure.summary: Segment 25 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## Is it safe for me to take ibuprofen, aspirin, or other over-the-counter painkillers?
For anyone with Chronic Kidney Disease, a class of painkillers called NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs) is generally considered unsafe. This group includes common medications like ibuprofen, naproxen, and high-dose aspirin. These drugs work by restricting blood flow to reduce inflammation, but in doing so, they also severely restrict the essential blood flow to your kidneys, which can cause sudden and permanent damage.

If you are dealing with a headache, joint pain, or a fever, acetaminophen (often known as paracetamol) is typically the safest over-the-counter option for kidney patients. It is processed primarily by the liver rather than the kidneys. However, it must still be taken at the correct dosage.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 26
structure.summary: Segment 26 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Even with "safe" medications, the golden rule of kidney disease is to never start a new over-the-counter drug, cough syrup, or painkiller without checking with your nephrologist first. Your care team needs to ensure it won't interact with your current prescriptions or put unnecessary strain on your remaining kidney function.

## Are there any vitamins or herbal supplements that are good for kidney health?
While the idea of a "natural" kidney supplement is appealing, herbal remedies and unregulated supplements can actually be incredibly dangerous for CKD patients. Many over-the-counter herbal treatments contain hidden heavy metals, toxic compounds, or extremely high levels of potassium and phosphorus that your compromised kidneys simply cannot filter out.

Standard multivitamins can also be problematic. They often contain high doses of fat-soluble vitamins (like Vitamin A, E, and K) which can build up to toxic levels in your body when your kidneys aren't working at full capacity.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 27
structure.summary: Segment 27 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
If you need a vitamin supplement, your doctor will prescribe a specific "renal vitamin." These are specially formulated to replace the exact water-soluble vitamins (like B and C) that are often lost during treatments like dialysis, without adding any of the minerals you need to avoid. Always bring every bottle of supplements or traditional remedies to your clinic visits so your doctor can verify they are safe for you.

## How do I know when it’s finally time to start dialysis?
Starting dialysis is rarely based on a single number or a specific date on the calendar. While doctors generally look at starting when your eGFR drops between 10 and 15, the decision is driven heavily by how you are actually feeling.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 28
structure.summary: Segment 28 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
Your care team will look for persistent signs of "uremia"—the toxic buildup of waste in your blood. If you are experiencing severe nausea, vomiting, a complete loss of appetite, dangerous fluid buildup in your lungs, or uncontrollable fatigue, it is usually a strong clinical sign that your kidneys can no longer keep up and you need the support of dialysis.

It is a shared decision between you and your nephrologist. Ideally, the conversation about dialysis starts months before you actually need it, allowing you time to get a vascular access (like a fistula) placed or a peritoneal dialysis catheter surgically prepared so you are ready when your body signals that it's time.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 29
structure.summary: Segment 29 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## What is the difference between hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis?
Hemodialysis (HD) is the most common form of treatment and involves using an artificial kidney machine to filter your blood outside of your body. This usually requires visiting a dialysis center three times a week for about four hours per session. During the treatment, needles are placed into a specially created access point in your arm (a fistula or graft) to safely cycle your blood through the machine's filter.

Peritoneal dialysis (PD), on the other hand, is a treatment you can manage yourself at home. It uses the natural lining of your own abdomen (the peritoneum) to filter waste. A cleansing fluid called dialysate is infused into your belly through a soft catheter, left there to absorb toxins, and then drained.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 30
structure.summary: Segment 30 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
PD is an excellent first-line option because it empowers you to take charge of your own care, often allowing for a more flexible schedule, a less restricted diet, and the ability to preserve your remaining kidney function a bit longer. Because it is done daily (or nightly while you sleep), it closely mimics the natural, continuous work of healthy kidneys.

## Can I still go on vacation or travel if I am on dialysis?
Yes, you absolutely can travel while on dialysis! A diagnosis of kidney failure does not mean you are permanently grounded, but it does require careful, proactive planning to ensure your treatments continue seamlessly while you are away from home.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 31
structure.summary: Segment 31 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
If you are on in-center hemodialysis, you or your social worker will need to locate a dialysis center at your destination and book "transient" treatment slots several weeks or even months in advance. You will need to send your medical records ahead of time so the destination clinic knows exactly what settings and medications you require.

If you are on peritoneal dialysis, traveling is generally much simpler. You can pack your bags with your manual exchange supplies, or if you are going for a longer trip, you can arrange with your supply company to have your dialysate fluid and cycler machine shipped directly to your hotel or family member's home.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 32
structure.summary: Segment 32 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text:
## How does the kidney transplant waitlist work, and how long does it usually take?
A kidney transplant is often the best long-term treatment for kidney failure, but it requires a rigorous medical workup to ensure your heart and body are strong enough for the surgery and the lifelong immunosuppressant medications that follow. Once you pass the medical evaluation, you are placed on the national deceased donor waitlist.

The wait time for a deceased donor kidney can vary wildly—often taking anywhere from three to seven years, depending heavily on your blood type and regional availability. The list is not a simple "first-come, first-served" line; organs are matched based on complex factors like genetic tissue typing, blood type compatibility, and time spent on the list.

structure.title: Kidney_FAQ.md - Part 33
structure.summary: Segment 33 of Kidney_FAQ.md
structure.text: However, you can entirely bypass this long waitlist if you have a living donor. A healthy family member, spouse, or even a close friend can donate one of their kidneys to you. Living donor transplants not only happen much faster, but the kidneys often work immediately and last significantly longer than those from deceased donors.

## INTRODUCTION
Rhabdomyolysis is a syndrome characterized by muscle necrosis and the release of intracellular muscle constituents into the circulation. 
## PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

1. The final common pathway for injury is an **increase in intracellular free ionized cytoplasmic and mitochondrial calcium**. This may be caused by depletion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the cellular source of energy, and/or by direct injury and rupture of the plasma membrane
2. The increased intracellular calcium leads to **activation of proteases**, increased skeletal muscle cell contractility, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the production of reactive oxygen species, resulting in skeletal muscle cell death
3. Myoglobin contains heme, which is nephrotoxic.

## CLASSIFICATION
1. Traumatic or muscle compression (eg, crush syndrome or prolonged immobilization)
2. Nontraumatic exertional (eg, marked exertion in untrained individuals, eccentric exercises, hyperthermia, or metabolic and other myopathies)
3. Nontraumatic nonexertional (eg, drugs or toxins, infections, or electrolyte disorders)

**Acquired (eg, trauma, drugs, physical exertion) or inherited (eg, muscular dystrophies, metabolic and mitochondrial disorders, sickle cell trait)**
## EPIDEMIOLOGY
Incidence — The true incidence of rhabdomyolysis is unknown, mainly due to its highly variable presentation and underrecognition and reporting of mild cases 

Most frequently associated clinical conditions included trauma (26 percent), immobilization (18 percent), sepsis (10 percent), vascular surgery (8 percent), and cardiac surgery (6 percent)

Up to 60 percent of patients had more than one etiologic factor. 
Underlying myopathy or muscle metabolic defects were seen in 10 percent of the cases
## Risk factors 
1. Male sex
2. Age <10 years and >60 years
3. Body mass index >40 kg/m2
4. History of prior heat injury
5. Low premorbid physical fitness
6. Chronic use of lipid-lowering drugs
7. Dehydration

### TRAUMA OR DIRECT MUSCLE INJURY

1. Crush syndrome 
2. Prolonged immobilization — Prolonged immobilization due to coma of any cause, sedation or incapacitation (eg, drug intoxication, stroke, hip fracture), or surgery can cause rhabdomyolysis from **unrelieved pressure on body regions**
3. Compression of blood vessels — Application of tourniquets, surgical clamps, splints, or even pneumatic compression devices.
4. Compartment syndrome 
5. Electrical injury and severe burn injury  
6. Physical restraint

### NONTRAUMATIC EXERTIONAL

### NONTRAUMATIC EXERTIONAL

1. Physical exertion and exercise — Rhabdomyolysis may arise from physical exertion, particularly when one or more of the following risk factors is present:
2. Severe heat and humidity 
3. Impaired heat loss
4. Hypokalemia 
5. Sickle cell trait 
6. Seizures and other hyperkinetic states :Delirium tremens, Psychotic agitation, Amphetamine overdose

### Inherited disorders 
1. Metabolic:  Glycogen metabolism disorders (eg, McArdle disease), Lipid metabolism disorders (eg, fatty acid oxidation disorders), 
Mitochondrial disorders-Pathogenic gene variants that alter gene expression (_MLIP_), impair muscle contraction (_MYH1_), disrupt excitation-contraction coupling and calcium handling (_OBSCN_), or alter SERCA2 function leading to cytosolic calcium overload (_ATP2A2_).

2. Muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies
3. Thermal extremes and dysregulation — Rhabdomyolysis may occur with hyperthermia associated with exertional heat stroke  
4. Malignant hyperthermia 
5. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome  

### NONEXERTIONAL AND NONTRAUMATIC

1. Drugs :
	1. Lipid-lowering drugs (statins and fibrates)
	2. antipsychotics, serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors, valproate, colchicine
	3. Antibiotics: Amphotericin B, Linezolid, Meropenem, Piptaz, Ciproloxacin, Septran, vasopressin

2. Drugs of abuse —  Cocaine, Amphetamines and methamphetamines, Heroin
3. Immobilization
4. Toxins —  Snake venoms,  bee stings, Mushroom poisoning
5. Infections : 
	1. influenza A and B, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr, herpes simplex, parainfluenza, adenovirus, echovirus, HIV, and cytomegalovirus 
	2.  Clostridium_, _Coxiella burnetii_ (Q fever), ehrlichiosis, _Escherichia coli_, _Legionella_, leptospirosis, _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Salmonella_, staphylococcal infection, _Streptococcus_, tularemia, and bacterial pyomyositis 
	3. Malaria caused by _Plasmodium falciparum_ 
6. Electrolyte disorders : hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia, DKA
7. Endocrine disorders — DKA, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytomaHypothyroidism.Hypothyroid myopathy manifests additionally with mild proximal muscle weakness, muscle hypertrophy, and myoedema. 
8. Inflammatory myopathies — Rhabdomyolysis has only rarely been described in patients with the inflammatory myopathies, dermatomyositis and polymyositis

**Statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) can have a subacute to acute onset with very elevated CK levels**

### CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS


1. Triad of **myalgias, muscle weakness, and red to brown urine** due to myoglobinuria. (1-10% cases) 
2. Urine — Dark-colored urine (red to brown, "tea-colored," "cola-colored") is one of the classic signs of rhabdomyolysis  but it occurs in ≤10 percent of cases.

Myoglobin, a heme-containing respiratory protein, is released from damaged muscle in parallel with CK. Myoglobin is a monomer that is not significantly protein bound and is therefore rapidly excreted in the urine, often resulting in the production of red to brown urine. 

It appears in the urine when the **plasma concentration exceeds 1.5 mg/dL**
Visible changes in the urine only occur once urine levels exceed from approximately **100 to 300 mg/dL**

### Fluid and electrolyte
1. Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia
2. Hypocalcemia- first few days because of entry into damaged myocytes and both deposition of calcium salts in damaged muscle and decreased bone responsiveness to parathyroid hormone
3. During the recovery phase, serum calcium levels return to normal and may rebound to significantly elevated levels due to the release of calcium from injured muscle, mild secondary hyperparathyroidism from the acute renal failure, and an increase in calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
4. Severe hyperuricemia  
5. Metabolic acidosis is common, and an increased anion gap may be present.

### EVALUATION AND DIAGNOSIS

The examination should focus on signs that suggest muscle injury, including muscle weakness and tenderness, limb edema, and evidence of trauma or compartment syndrome.

1. Serum CK, the standard biomarker 
2. Urinalysis of a fresh urine specimen,

1. Serum CK, the standard biomarker 
2. Urinalysis of a fresh urine specimen,  

**While no absolute cut-off value for CK elevation is defined, serum CK is usually >5000 units/L with nonexertional rhabdomyolysis and >10,000 units/L with exertional rhabdomyolysis, but ranges from approximately 1500 to over 100,000 units/L**

**Following muscle injury**
1. Serum CK begins to rise within 2 to 12 hours, 
2. Maximum within 24 to 72 hours, and usually 
3. Declines within three to five days 

*CK has a serum half-life of approximately 1.5 days (d/w Myoglobin has a half-life of only two to three hours) and declines at a relatively constant rate of approximately 40 to 50 percent of the previous day's value 
In patients whose CK does not decline as expected, continued muscle injury, an underlying muscle disease, or the development of a compartment syndrome may be present*

The CK is generally entirely or almost entirely of the MM or skeletal muscle fraction; a small proportion of the total CK may be from the MB or myocardial fraction. The presence of MB reflects the small amount found in skeletal muscle rather than the presence of myocardial disease.

### Urine findings and myoglobinuria:
1. Urine supernatant tests positive for heme by dipstick after centrifugation, while the plasma has a normal color.
2. Urinary sediment shows few or no RBCs (<3 RBCs per high-powered field)
3. It is not unusual for CK levels to remain elevated in the absence of myoglobinuria
#### GGT and bilirubin are not found in muscle, demonstrating a CK elevation and a normal serum GGT or bilirubin level will help to distinguish from muscle pathology Vs liver pathology

### MANAGEMENT
1. Treatment of rhabdomyolysis is supportive 
2. Prevention of heme pigment-induced acute kidney injury, correction of fluid and electrolyte abnormalities, and management of complications

### Prevention of AKI in Rhabdomyolysis
1. Correction of volume depletion if present
2. Prevention of intratubular cast formation

**The plasma CK concentration correlates with the severity of muscle injury, and concentrations >5000 units/L identify patients with rhabdomyolysis who are at risk for the development of AKI**

### Volume administration
1. Patients with rhabdomyolysis, use isotonic saline- initiated at a rate of 1 to 2 L/hour.
2. Titrate the rate of IV fluids to target a goal urine output of approximately 200 to 300 mL/hour while avoiding volume overload
3. Fluid repletion should be continued until plasma CK levels decrease to ≤5000 units/L and continue to fall
4. Patients with hemolysis, we continue fluids until the lactate dehydrogenase level decreases to <1.5 times the upper limit of normal and the hemoglobin is stable over at least a six-hour period

**Bicarbonate in selected patients**
Provided that the following conditions are met:
	1. Hypocalcemia is not present
	2. Arterial pH is less than 7.5
	3. Serum bicarbonate is less than 30 mEq/L

Monitoring on Bicarbonate
	1. Arterial pH and serum calcium should be monitored every two hours
	2. Bicarbonate infusion should be discontinued if the urine pH does not rise above 6.5 after three to four hours, if the patient develops symptomatic hypocalcemia, if the arterial pH exceeds 7.5, or if the serum bicarbonate exceeds 30 mEq/L

### Not recommended
1. Mannitol for forced diuresis- can cause more AKI
2. Loop Diuretics- Can worsen hypocalcemia, hypovolemia, increase the risk of cast formation
3. Dialysis -for removal of myoglobin, hemoglobin, or uric acid

# Prospective Study on Individualized Dose Adjustment of Tolvaptan Based on Urinary Osmolality in Patients with ADPKD

**Title of the paper**: Prospective Study on Individualized Dose Adjustment of Tolvaptan Based on Urinary Osmolality in Patients with ADPKD

**DOI**: [10.1016/j.ekir.2024.01.020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2024.01.020)

**Authors**: F.J. Roca Oporto, C. Andrades Gómez, G. Montilla Cosano, A. Luna Aguilera, José L. Rocha

**Journal**: Kidney International Reports, 2024

**PubMed Link**: [Link to the study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37281423/)

---

**Journal**: Kidney International Reports, 2024

**PubMed Link**: [Link to the study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37281423/)

---

## Abstract of the Study:
This prospective cohort study investigates the feasibility of individualized dose adjustments of Tolvaptan based on urinary osmolality (OsmU) in patients with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) experiencing rapid disease progression. Tolvaptan treatment started at 45/15 mg and was adjusted to maintain OsmU below 200 mOsm/kg. Primary outcomes measured were the decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and the occurrence of renal events. The study demonstrated a significant reduction in eGFR decline and fewer side effects with individualized dosing compared to standard protocols.

---

## Notes:

---

## Notes:

### **Bottom Line**
- **Effective Patency Maintenance**: Individualized Tolvaptan dosing based on OsmU reduces eGFR decline and maintains lower dropout rates.
- **Significant Benefits**: Lower dose requirements and reduced side effects compared to standard dosing protocols.

### **Brief Introduction of the Study**
- **Context**: ADPKD is a genetic disorder causing kidney cysts and progressive renal function loss. Tolvaptan is known to slow this progression, but optimal dosing strategies remain unclear.
- **Objective**: Assess the feasibility of using OsmU to guide individualized Tolvaptan dosing in ADPKD patients.

### **Design of the Study**
- **Population**: 40 ADPKD patients with rapid disease progression from Hospital Universitario Virgen del Rocío, Seville, Spain.
- **Methodology**: Prospective cohort study with initial Tolvaptan dose set at 45/15 mg, adjusted upwards to maintain OsmU below 200 mOsm/kg. Patients were followed for a 3-year period, with regular monitoring of eGFR, OsmU, and adverse events.

### **Baseline Characteristics of Study Population**
- **Demographics**:
  - Mean age: 45 years (± 7 years)
  - Gender distribution: 47% male
  - Mean body mass index (BMI): 26 kg/m² (± 4.5)
- **Clinical Baselines**:
  - Mean baseline eGFR: 51.05 ml/min per 1.73 m² (± 12.52)
  - Hypertension prevalence: 82%
  - CKD Stages: Majority were in stage 3 (78%)
  - Mayo Clinical Classification: Predominantly 1C (53%)

### **Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria**
- **Inclusion**:
  - Patients aged ≥18 years with ADPKD
  - CKD stages 2-4
  - Evidence of rapid disease progression: eGFR decline ≥5 ml/min per 1.73 m² in the previous year or ≥2.5 ml/min per 1.73 m² annually over the past 5 years
- **Exclusion**:
  - Patients with other renal pathologies
  - Lack of consent for participation

### **Clinical Presentation of Patients**
- **Symptoms**:
  - Polyuria: All patients experienced increased urine output
  - High baseline urinary osmolality indicating high vasopressin activity
  - Hypertension was prevalent among the cohort

### **Detailed Study Findings with Key Interventions**
- **Urinary Osmolality Management**:
  - Maintained below 200 mOsm/kg in the majority of patients throughout the study.
  - Significant reduction observed within the first month of treatment.
- **Tolvaptan Dose Adjustments**:
  - Initial dose: 45/15 mg.
  - Mean dose: 64 mg (± 10 mg), with dose increases to 60/30 mg in some patients.
  - No patients required the maximum dose of 90/30 mg.

### **Primary Outcomes of the Study**
- **eGFR Decline**:
  - Significant reduction in the annual decline of eGFR.
  - Pre-treatment annual decline: -7.71 ml/min per 1.73 m² (± 4.15)
  - Post-treatment annual decline: -3.05 ml/min per 1.73 m² (± 2.41)
  - Represents a >50% reduction in the rate of decline.

### **Secondary Outcomes of the Study**
- **Secondary Renal Events**:
  - Occurred in 40% of patients.
  - Most common complications: uncontrolled hypertension and episodes of complicated cysts.
  - Higher baseline OsmU correlated with secondary events.

### **Detailed Results with Statistical Summary**
- **eGFR Changes**:
  - Significant improvement in eGFR slope post-treatment.
  - Mean annual decline pre-treatment: -7.71 ml/min per 1.73 m² (± 4.15)
  - Mean annual decline post-treatment: -3.05 ml/min per 1.73 m² (± 2.41)
- **OsmU Levels**:
  - Significant reduction within the first month (mean decrease of 220 mOsm/kg).
  - Maintained below 200 mOsm/kg consistently.

### **Subgroup Analysis and Adverse Events**
- **Dose Response**:
  - No significant differences in primary outcomes between patients on 45/15 mg and those on 60/30 mg.
- **Adverse Events**:
  - Hyperuricemia: 18%
  - Hypernatremia: 11%, with a maximum sodium level of 148 mEq/l
  - Polyuria: Reported in all patients, with median diuresis of 6000 ml/day
  - No cases of hepatotoxicity obs

### **Subgroup Analysis and Adverse Events**
- **Dose Response**:
  - No significant differences in primary outcomes between patients on 45/15 mg and those on 60/30 mg.
- **Adverse Events**:
  - Hyperuricemia: 18%
  - Hypernatremia: 11%, with a maximum sodium level of 148 mEq/l
  - Polyuria: Reported in all patients, with median diuresis of 6000 ml/day
  - No cases of hepatotoxicity observed.
  - Two patients (5%) discontinued due to aquaretic effects.

### **Statistical Tests Used and Interpretation**
- **Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves**:
  - Used to estimate renal event-free survival over the study period.
- **Log-Rank Test (Mantel-Cox)**:
  - Employed to compare survival curves between different groups.
- **Cox Regression Models**:
  - Used to identify factors associated with survival-free renal events.
- **Mixed ANOVA**:
  - Assessed changes in eGFR over time and between different Tolvaptan dose groups.

### **Main Weaknesses of the Paper**
- **Non-Randomized Design**:
  - The absence of a control group limits the ability to draw direct comparisons.
- **Sample Size**:
  - The study was conducted at a single center with a relatively small number of patients.
- **Biomarker Measurement**:
  - Did not include measurements of plasma copeptin levels, which could provide additional insights into treatment efficacy.

### **Issues Not Addressed and Further Research Questions**
- **Long-Term Outcomes**:
  - Further studies are necessary to validate long-term benefits and optimal dosing strategies.
- **Generalizability**:
  - Larger, multi-center randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm findings and improve generalizability.

structure.title: how to prevent kidney disease?
structure.summary: You can protect your kidneys by preventing or managing health conditions that cause kidney damage, such as diabetes and high blood pressure.
structure.text:
You can protect your kidneys by preventing or managing health conditions that cause kidney damage, such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

**Key Steps to Keep Your Kidneys Healthy:**
1. **Choose Healthy Foods:** Focus on fresh fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy.
2. **Limit Salt and Sugar:** Aim for less than 2,300 mg of sodium per day. 
3. **Be Active:** Aim for 30 minutes or more of physical activity on most days.
4. **Healthy Weight:** Work with your team to reach or stay at a healthy weight.
5. **Sleep:** Aim for 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night.
6. **Stop Smoking:** Quitting smoking is one of the best things you can do for your heart and kidneys.
7. **Limit Alcohol:** Stick to 1 drink per day (women) or 2 (men).
8. **Manage Conditions:** Keep your blood glucose and blood pressure close to goals.
9. **Be Cautious with Meds:** Avoid regular use of NSAIDs like Ibuprofen/Naproxen. 
10. **Stress Management:** Explore meditation, yoga, or laughter therapy.

*Early kidney disease has no symptoms. Getting tested is the only way to know.*

structure.title: what is ckd?
structure.summary: **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** is when the kidneys stop working as well as they should. Normally, the kidneys filter blood and remove waste, but in
structure.text:
**Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** is when the kidneys stop working as well as they should. Normally, the kidneys filter blood and remove waste, but in CKD, this ability is slowly lost.

**Key Facts:**
- **Progression:** If left unchecked, CKD can lead to end-stage kidney disease (kidney failure).
- **Goal:** The primary goal is to "Hit the Brakes" to keep CKD from getting worse through medical and lifestyle changes.
- **Diet:** Dietary needs change significantly between early CKD and those on dialysis.

structure.title: common causes of ckd
structure.summary: The two biggest causes of kidney failure are:
structure.text:
The two biggest causes of kidney failure are:
1. **Diabetes:** High blood sugar damages the kidneys' tiny filters over time.
2. **High Blood Pressure:** Puts extra pressure on kidney blood vessels, wearing them out.

*Other causes include autoimmune diseases (Lupus), genetic conditions (PKD), and recurring kidney stones.*

structure.title: what are kidney failure stages?
structure.summary: Kidney health is assessed through two tests: **eGFR** (filtering rate) and **uACR** (urine protein).
structure.text:
Kidney health is assessed through two tests: **eGFR** (filtering rate) and **uACR** (urine protein).

| Stage | Description | eGFR |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Stage 1** | Normal function with damage | 90+ |
| **Stage 2** | Mild loss of function | 60-89 |
| **Stage 3** | Moderate loss of function | 30-59 |
| **Stage 4** | Severe loss of function | 15-29 |
| **Stage 5** | Kidney Failure (ESRD) | <15 |

*Stage 1 & 2 is the "Golden Window" for prevention. Stage 3 is where you must "Hit the Brakes" to avoid dialysis.*

structure.title: your kidneys explained: guide to health and failure
structure.summary: Our kidneys are the body's super-efficient cleaning system, working 24/7 to filter waste, balance fluids, and keep blood pressure in check.
structure.text:
Our kidneys are the body's super-efficient cleaning system, working 24/7 to filter waste, balance fluids, and keep blood pressure in check.

**Two Main Types of Kidney Trouble:**
1. **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** Sudden damage occurring over hours or days. Often **reversible** if treated quickly. Causes include severe dehydration, heart problems, or infections.
2. **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD):** A slow, gradual loss of function over months or years, usually caused by long-term conditions like **Diabetes** and **High Blood Pressure**.

**Warning Signs:**
- Changes in urination (frequency, foam, or blood).
- Swelling (puffy eyes, swollen hands/feet).
- Constant fatigue and weakness.
- Loss appetite, nausea, or vomiting.

**How Doctors Diagnose:**
- **Blood Tests:** Checking creatinine and calculating your **eGFR** (the filtering score).
- **Urine Tests:** Looking for protein (albumin).
- **Imaging:** Ultrasounds or CT scans to check for blockages.
- **Biopsy:** Taking a tiny sample of tissue for microscopic study.

structure.title: hitting the brakes on ckd
structure.summary: Being diagnosed with CKD can feel overwhelming, but today we have more tools and knowledge than ever before to "hit the brakes" and slow down its prog
structure.text:
Being diagnosed with CKD can feel overwhelming, but today we have more tools and knowledge than ever before to "hit the brakes" and slow down its progression.

### 1. The Power of Lifestyle
- **Eat for Your Kidneys:** Focus on fresh fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. Limit salt to control blood pressure.
- **Get Moving:** Aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity (walking, swimming, cycling) on most days.
- **Harmful Habits:** Quitting smoking and limiting alcohol reduce significant kidney strain.
- **Mind Your Mind:** Stress management through yoga, meditation, or **laughter therapy and prayer** are vital for BP control.

### 2. Modern Medicines (The Game-Changer)
Breakthroughs like **SGLT2 inhibitors** provide **direct protection** to both the heart and kidneys, significantly slowing CKD progression beyond just managing symptoms.

### 3. Smarter Healthcare
- **Precision Medicine:** Tailored treatment plans based on your individual profile.
- **Telemedicine:** Remote monitoring allows for closer care from home.
- **AI Risk Prediction:** Analytics help doctors predict who is at higher risk for proactive intervention.

structure.title: high bp's secret victim: the kidneys
structure.summary: High blood pressure is one of the top causes of kidney failure. It is often a "silent killer" because you may not feel anything until serious damage i
structure.text:
High blood pressure is one of the top causes of kidney failure. It is often a "silent killer" because you may not feel anything until serious damage is done.

**The Filter Under Pressure:**
Imagine your kidneys are advanced water purifiers. High BP is like forcing water through those fine filters with extreme force every day. Over time, the fragile filtering units wear out and break down. 

**Small Steps to Protect Your Kidneys:**
1. **Go Easy on Salt:** Limit packaged snacks (chips, pickles/achar).
2. **Hydrate:** Drink 6-8 glasses of water daily to flush waste.
3. **Move:** 30 minutes of brisk walking is powerful medicine.
4. **Know Your Numbers:** Check your BP regularly and get a yearly Kidney Function Test (KFT).

structure.title: are you unknowingly harming your kidneys? 10 habits
structure.summary: Many everyday habits can silently cause kidney damage over time.
structure.text:
Many everyday habits can silently cause kidney damage over time.

1. **Ignoring Thirst:** Dehydration increases stone and UTI risk.
2. **Too Much Salt (Namak):** Found in pickles, papad, and chips; raises BP.
3. **Sweet Tooth:** Sugar fuels diabetes, the #1 cause of kidney failure.
4. **'Wait and Hold':** Holding urine encourages bacterial growth/infections.
5. **Painkiller Abuse:** Overuse of NSAIDs (Ibuprofen/Diclofenac) harms kidney tissue.
6. **Processed Foods:** High in sodium and phosphorus additives.
7. **Excess Alcohol:** Dehydrates the body and strains filtering.
8. **Smoking:** Damages blood vessels and reduces kidney blood flow.
9. **Sit-Down Lifestyle:** Physical inactivity fuels obesity and hypertension.
10. **Lack of Sleep:** The body repairs kidney tissue during deep sleep.

structure.title: kidney damage: is it possible to reverse?
structure.summary: Whether kidney damage can be reversed depends on the stage and the cause.
structure.text:
Whether kidney damage can be reversed depends on the stage and the cause.

**1. Early Stages (Hope for Reversal):**
In Stage 1 or 2, if damage is from a temporary cause (infection, dehydration, medicine), the kidneys can often return to normal function by treating the root cause.

**2. Middle Stage (Halt the Damage):**
In Stage 3, complete reversal is rare, but you can "Hit the Brakes." The goal is to slow or stop the disease from getting worse through diet and medication.

**3. Late Stages (Help is Needed):**
In Stages 4 & 5, damage is usually irreversible. Focus shifts to medical support like dialysis or preparing for a transplant.

*Early detection is everything. Proactive management can help you preserve function for many years.*

structure.title: weight and blood pressure: the twin threats
structure.summary: Obesity (being overweight) and Hypertension (high BP) are closely linked and act as "twin threats" to your kidneys.
structure.text:
Obesity (being overweight) and Hypertension (high BP) are closely linked and act as "twin threats" to your kidneys.

**How Extra Weight Raises BP:**
- **More Work:** The heart has to pump harder to reach more body tissue.
- **Chemical Signals:** Body fat releases chemicals that cause inflammation.
- **Hormone Imbalance:** Being overweight can lead to insulin resistance.

**Taking Control Naturally:**
- **Eat Smart:** Fill half your plate with colorful vegetables. Use whole grains like whole wheat roti.
- **Move Every Day:** A 30-minute brisk walk or yoga (Pranayama) is highly effective.
- **Prioritize Sleep:** 7-8 hours helps regulate weight-inducing stress hormones.

structure.title: how much water do i really need?
structure.summary: Hydration needs follow different rules for different people:
structure.text:
Hydration needs follow different rules for different people:
1. **For Stone Prevention:** Drink plenty (2.5 to 3 liters) to dilute minerals.
2. **For Advanced CKD:** You may need **fluid restriction**. If kidneys can't flush water, it builds up, causing heart strain and swelling.

*Always follow the specific fluid chart provided by your nephrologist.*

structure.title: what are the symptoms of kidney disease?
structure.summary: Kidney disease is a "Silent Killer," but watch for these warning signs:
structure.text:
Kidney disease is a "Silent Killer," but watch for these warning signs:
- **Changes in Peeing:** Foamy urine, blood in urine, or peeing more at night.
- **Swelling (Edema):** Puffy eyes, swollen ankles or hands.
- **Fatigue:** Feeling weak because of anemia (low red blood cells).
- **Breath Issues:** Fluid in the lungs or anemia.
- **Skin Itching:** Waste buildup (uremia) in the blood.
- **Metallic Taste:** Ammonia-like breath or bad taste in food.

structure.title: kidney stones vs kidney failure?
structure.summary: They are very different conditions:
structure.text:
They are very different conditions:
- **Kidney Stones:** A temporary "pebble in the pipe" causing intense pain. Once passed, function usually remains normal.
- **Kidney Failure:** The entire "filter system" breaks down. A silent, systemic condition that requires long-term care.

structure.title: preparing for doctor visit
structure.summary: Better planning leads to better care:
structure.text:
Better planning leads to better care:
- **Ask:** What is my GFR? What is my urine protein? 
- **Treatment:** Do I need to change my diet? Should I see a dietitian?
- **Support:** Bring a friend or family member to help take notes and remember instructions.

structure.title: who is on my healthcare team?
structure.summary: Kidney care is a team effort involving:
structure.text:
Kidney care is a team effort involving:
- **Nephrologist:** Kidney specialist.
- **Primary Doctor:** Manages BP and diabetes.
- **Renal Dietitian:** Creates custom eating plans.
- **Social Worker:** Helps with costs and dialysis applications.
- **Pharmacist:** Checks for kidney-safe medicines.

structure.title: how do kidneys work?
structure.summary: Kidneys are your body's "Master Chemists":
structure.text:
Kidneys are your body's "Master Chemists":
1. **Filters:** Over 1 million **nephrons** clean about a liter of blood every minute.
2. **Water Balance:** They remove excess water or retain it when needed.
3. **Minerals:** They balance sodium, potassium, and calcium for heart and bone health.
4. **Hormones:** They produce hormones for blood pressure and red blood cell production.

structure.title: the dangerous trio: diabetes, high bp, and kidneys
structure.summary: In India, diabetes and high blood pressure (BP) are the leading causes of kidney failure, responsible for about 7 out of 10 cases.
structure.text:
In India, diabetes and high blood pressure (BP) are the leading causes of kidney failure, responsible for about 7 out of 10 cases.

**How They Attack:**
- **Diabetes:** High blood sugar acts like a "sugary syrup" that clogs and damages the tiny holes in your kidney's filters.
- **High BP:** Like blasting water through a fine strainer with too much force, weakening the delicate mesh over time.
- **The Double Attack:** Having both can double the risk of kidney failure, creating a vicious cycle where damaged kidneys raise BP further.

**5-Point Protection Plan:**
1. **Control Your Numbers:** Keep HbA1c and BP within targets.
2. **Yearly Check-Up:** Get a blood (KFT) and urine test every year.
3. **Kidney-Friendly Diet:** Limit salt (bhujia/pickles), sugar, and fried foods.
4. **Stay Active:** 30 mins of daily walking or yoga.
5. **Medicine Safety:** Avoid overuse of painkillers and unverified local remedies.

structure.title: the silent worker: yearly kidney check-up
structure.summary: Kidneys are "silent workers" that rarely complain until damage is severe. A yearly check-up is the only way to catch issues early.
structure.text:
Kidneys are "silent workers" that rarely complain until damage is severe. A yearly check-up is the only way to catch issues early.

**What's in a Check-Up?**
1. **Blood Test:** Measures how efficiently your filters clean the blood (eGFR).
2. **Urine Test:** Looks for tiny amounts of protein leaking out (albuminuria).
3. **BP Check:** High blood pressure is a top enemy of the kidneys.

**Why Early Detection Matters:**
Finding a problem early puts **you** in the driver's seat. You can often slow or stop damage with simple dietary changes or better sugar/BP control. Modern medicine is most effective when issues are found before symptoms appear.

structure.title: common kidney silent killers
structure.summary: Kidney diseases can often progress without noticeable symptoms, making them **"silent killers."** Here are common conditions and factors that contribu
structure.text:
Kidney diseases can often progress without noticeable symptoms, making them **"silent killers."** Here are common conditions and factors that contribute to kidney damage:

**1. Silent Stones**
Kidney stones can exist without symptoms for years, yet they can cause significant kidney damage when they obstruct urinary flow.

**2. Uncontrolled High Blood Pressure**
Severe, uncontrolled hypertension, especially at a young age, is a common early indicator of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD).

**3. Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD)**
This inherited condition is a leading cause of CKD. Many individuals may not show symptoms until later in life, but it can lead to severe complications.

**4. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)**
Early stages are often asymptomatic; regular screening is essential for those at risk (e.g., those with diabetes or a family history of kidney disease).

**5. Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)**
Recurrent UTIs can lead to kidney damage if not treated promptly, especially in children.

**6. Over-the-Counter Medications**
Many common medications, such as **NSAIDs** and certain painkillers, can cause kidney damage if taken excessively or without medical supervision.

**7. Dehydration and Hypotension**
Conditions leading to dehydration, such as diarrhea or vomiting, can significantly impair kidney function if not addressed quickly.

### Prevention Tips
- **Regular Check-ups:** Monitor blood pressure and kidney function regularly, especially if you have risk factors.
- **Healthy Lifestyle:** Maintain a balanced diet, stay hydrated, and engage in regular physical activity to support kidney health.

*If you have concerns about your kidney health, it’s essential to consult your nephrologist for personalized advice and treatment options.*

structure.title: should i be worried about blood in my urine?
structure.summary: Seeing blood in your urine (**hematuria**) can be scary, but it is not always a sign of a serious condition. However, you should **always see a doctor
structure.text:
Seeing blood in your urine (**hematuria**) can be scary, but it is not always a sign of a serious condition. However, you should **always see a doctor or nurse** to find the cause.

Blood can come from the kidneys (where urine is produced) or anywhere along the urinary tract (ureters, bladder, or urethra).

structure.title: what causes blood in the urine?
structure.summary: Hematuria can be caused by many different factors, ranging from minor to serious:
structure.text:
Hematuria can be caused by many different factors, ranging from minor to serious:

**Common Causes:**
- **Infections:** Bladder infections (cystitis) or kidney infections (pyelonephritis).
- **Kidney Stones:** Small mineral deposits that irritate the urinary tract.
- **Enlarged Prostate:** Common in older males (Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia).
- **Kidney Diseases:** Various conditions that affect the kidney's filters.
- **Injury:** Physical trauma to the kidney (e.g., from a fall or accident).

**Other Causes:**
- **Intense Exercise:** Strenuous physical activity can sometimes cause temporary blood in urine.
- **Cancer:** Uncommon, but can affect the bladder, prostate, or kidney (usually in people over 50).
- **Non-Blood Red Urine:** Certain foods (beets, food dyes) or medications can make urine look red or tea-colored without actual blood being present.

structure.title: will i need tests for blood in the urine?
structure.summary: Depending on your age and symptoms, your doctor may recommend several diagnostic tests:
structure.text:
Depending on your age and symptoms, your doctor may recommend several diagnostic tests:

**Diagnostic Methodology:**
- **Urine Tests:** To check for protein (a sign of kidney disease), infection, or specific cell types.
- **Blood Tests:** To check kidney function and look for systemic diseases.
- **Blood Pressure Check:** High BP can be both a cause and a sign of kidney problems.

**Imaging & Procedures:**
- **CT Scan or Ultrasound:** To create images of the kidneys and urinary tract to look for stones or growths.
- **Cystoscopy:** Using a thin camera (cystoscope) to look inside the bladder and urethra.
- **Kidney Biopsy:** Taking a tiny tissue sample to examine under a microscope if a specific kidney disease is suspected.

structure.title: will i need treatment for blood in the urine?
structure.summary: Treatment depends entirely on the underlying cause:
structure.text:
Treatment depends entirely on the underlying cause:

- **Infections:** Typically require **antibiotics**.
- **Kidney Stones:** May require fluids, pain meds, or procedures if they don't pass.
- **Exercise/Injury:** Often no treatment is needed, just rest and monitoring.
- **Chronic Conditions:** Managing blood pressure and using specific kidney-protective medications.

structure.title: when to call a doctor for blood in the urine?
